model.comments: This is the high effort version of the Claude Opus 4.7 model.

prompt: # Role - You are an AI competing in a gaming arena. # Objective - Write a complete Python file that provides the next move for a Checkers on an 8x8 board. - You must define a smart policy that is able to beat other policies in the arena. - You will be disqualified if you do not return a legal move string. Therefore, you must always return a legal move string. # Required API The provided python file must implement the following API: ```python def policy(my_men, my_kings, opp_men, opp_kings, color) -> tuple[tuple[int, int], tuple[int, int]]: ... ``` # State Representation - You are always the player to move. - `my_men` is a list of squares containing your regular pieces. - `my_kings` is a list of squares containing your kings. - `opp_men` is a list of squares containing opponent regular pieces. - `opp_kings` is a list of squares containing opponent kings. - `color` is your color: `'b'` for black which moves downwards (to lower row values) and `'w'` for white which moves upwards (to higher row values). - Squares use coordinates: row `0`-`7`, column `0`-`7`. - `(0, 0)` is the bottom-left corner; rows increase bottom-to-top and columns increase left-to-right. - Only dark squares are playable. # Action / Return Format - Return a move as a tuple: `((from_row, from_col), (to_row, to_col))`. - `from_row`, `to_row`, `from_col`, `to_col` are coordinates `0..7`. - (`from_row`, `from_col`) has to be a coordinate of a piece that is yours and (`to_row`, `to_col`) has to be the destination square.Return a legal move; captures are mandatory when available. # Constraints - You may use any standard Python imports, including numpy. - Your code is allowed 1 second of execution time on a modern 3GHz CPU. # Output Format Requirements - Output your strategy before providing the Python source code for your policy. - Output the Python source code for your policy surrounded by `...` tags. # Example Output The strategy for this policy is... ...
reasoning:
I'm outlining a checkers AI using alpha-beta search on an 8x8 board where black moves down and white moves up, with standard American checkers rules including mandatory captures, multi-jump sequences, and king promotion at the opposite end.

Now I'm clarifying the movement mechanics: men move diagonally forward one square, kings move diagonally in any direction one square, and captures involve jumping over opponent pieces to empty squares two squares away. I need to handle the edge case where a man becomes a king during a jump sequence—it stops jumping after promotion rather than continuing.

Setting up the core implementation... Writing the recursive capture logic... Refining the capture logic...

I need to make sure the destination square is actually empty—checking that it's not in the combined piece set, excluding already-captured pieces. The moving piece itself has left its starting position, so revisiting that square should be allowed. I'm also tracking when a piece becomes a king upon reaching the back row, and if that happens, the capture sequence ends there. Otherwise, I recursively search for additional captures from the new position, building up the full jump path and the set of captured pieces as I go. The key insight is that `all_pieces` should remain static—it's the opponent's pieces plus my own pieces minus the one currently moving.

Now I'm writing the main function that applies a move to the game state...

Implementing the evaluation function...

Building the alpha-beta search...

Wrapping it all together with iterative deepening and a time limit to keep the search from running too long, trying progressively deeper depths until we're close to the time cutoff.

Now I'm checking the API requirements—it looks like I just need to return the starting and ending positions as a tuple, even for multi-jump moves, which the judge should be able to resolve. I'm also reconsidering whether a transposition table would help, but with only a second of time, probably not worth the overhead. For the opening position with 12 pieces, depth 6 should be reachable. I need to make sure promotion during multi-jumps stops the sequence correctly, following standard American checkers rules.

Writing the capture logic... Still writing game logic... Continuing the iterative deepening search with alpha-beta pruning, I'm converting the piece positions to sets for faster lookups, then running a time-bounded search that progressively explores deeper move trees until the 0.8-second deadline approaches.

Now I'm catching a bug in my move validation logic—I need to ensure that landing squares are truly empty, not occupied by any pieces including those marked as captured, since captured pieces remain on the board until the sequence completes. I'm verifying the landing logic handles revisited squares correctly—since `my_pieces_except` excludes the starting position, the piece can return there, and intermediate squares become empty after the king leaves so they're valid landing spots too. The promotion rule is also correct: a man stops jumping once it reaches the king row, which my code implements properly. For the evaluation, I'm keeping it simple for now, and the negamax logic correctly returns -9999 when the opponent has no moves available. I should implement a smarter time budget using a timeout exception rather than a conservative threshold, since opening positions with many pieces could take around 0.5 seconds at depth 6.

I'm restructuring the iterative deepening to catch timeout exceptions and fall back to the best move from the last completed depth. Move ordering will help efficiency—I can sort captures by count to prioritize higher-capture moves first. Before finalizing, I need to trace through the state representation in the policy function to make sure the perspective is consistent after applying moves.
